statedGuarantee: AgentCgroup guarantees a RESOURCE-CONSUMPTION bound, not an action permission. Each agent workload maps to a cgroup v2 node with individual tool calls as ephemeral child nodes, so CPU and memory limits can be set per tool call while a workload-level budget still holds; enforcement runs in-kernel at the memcg allocation hook (memcg_bpf_ops) and the scheduler (sched_ext), applying graduated throttling (memory.high delays) and then cgroup.freeze in preference to OOM termination, so accumulated agent state survives. An advisory upward channel lets the agent declare expected need per tool call (AGENT_RESOURCE_HINT) and a downward channel injects natural-language feedback into stderr after a throttle or kill so the agent can retry with a cheaper strategy. The paper contains NO threat model, no adversary, and no security claim: 'isolation' throughout means multi-tenant PERFORMANCE isolation between co-located agent sessions, not confinement of a misbehaving or compromised agent.
advertisedRhetoric: "in-kernel enforcement via sched_ext and memcg_bpf_ops"; "AgentCgroup executes control logic directly at kernel cgroup enforcement points via eBPF, enabling microsecond-level reaction without user-kernel round trips"; "No application code is modified; isolation is achieved entirely through container cgroup boundaries and eBPF hooks."
tierSpan: a transparent bash wrapper intercepts each bash -c invocation, a common tool-call execution interface in agent frameworks, and creates an ephemeral child cgroup (tool_<pid>_<ts>/) for the duration of the command. The wrapper moves the tool process into this child cgroup
cheapestDefeat: TIER WORK, EXPLICIT. (1) GUARANTEE: a tool call and every process it spawns stay inside a per-tool-call cgroup whose memory/CPU limit is enforced in-kernel. (2) MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: not the kernel controller, but the USER-SPACE PLACEMENT step. Kernel enforcement only binds processes that are inside the ephemeral cgroup, and membership is established by a transparent bash wrapper that keys on the `bash -c` invocation form. (3) CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: do not invoke the tool as `bash -c`. A direct execve, a `sh -c`, a differently-formed `/bin/bash` call, or any non-Bash tool path (Read, Edit, Web search, and the sub-agent tool, the last being 17.3% of Haiku tool time) never enters an ephemeral cgroup, so the per-tool-call constraint the paper advertises never attaches. Cost: zero privilege, pure user space, no kernel interaction. A second, even cheaper defeat of the adaptive layer: declare AGENT_RESOURCE_HINT="memory:high" on every call, since the paper states declarations are advisory. (4) TIER DEFEATED: an application-level shim on one invocation form = T3. RESIDUAL, stated for fairness: a genuine T2 bound survives the bypass, because a bypassing process is still a descendant inside the parent workload cgroup and cgroup v2 membership is inherited across fork; the paper's memcg_bpf_ops is 'attached to the parent cgroup' and cgroup.kill 'terminates all processes while handling concurrent forks'. So the WORKLOAD-level ceiling is T2 while the TOOL-CALL-level control, the paper's headline granularity contribution, is T3. Weakest-link rule forces T3. Two further fragilities: the prototype requires out-of-tree memcg struct_ops patches 'currently under upstream review', and a task with write access to cgroup.procs inside a delegated container can move itself between sibling cgroups.
placementSpan: We use three agent traces run concurrently in separate cgroups: dask/dask#11628 as the HIGH-priority session (peak 421 MB, memory.high = max) and two instances of sigmavirus24/github3.py#673 as LOW-priority sessions (peak 406 MB each, memory.high = 400 MB). Under BPF, LOW cgroups are throttled when the HIGH cgroup experiences memory pressure

coverageSpans.E2: memcg_bpf_ops attached to the parent cgroup automatically applies to all child cgroups via cgroup v2 hierarchy inheritance, requiring no BPF code changes.
coverageSpans.E5: Resource fluctuations come almost entirely from subprocesses spawned by tool calls: test execution, dependency installation, and other operations raise memory to 500 MB-2 GB, then fall back to baseline.
coverageSpans.E7: In Haiku, Bash and the sub-agent tool (which delegates to a new agent instance) together account for over 90% of total tool execution time (80.6% and 17.3% respectively)

schneider.surrogate: A per-cgroup resource-consumption ceiling, which IS a safety property and IS monitorable: the memcg allocation hook and the sched_ext dispatch path are reference monitors sitting on every allocation and every scheduling decision, and the bad thing they prevent (an allocation that carries a cgroup past its limit) is observable on a single finite execution prefix. cgroup.freeze and cgroup.kill give the monitor a truncation primitive over the whole subtree, which is exactly the Schneider EM shape.
schneider.objective: Two advertised objectives sit outside that class. (a) 'improved multi-tenant isolation' - performance isolation is a relation BETWEEN executions of co-located tenants (tenant A's latency must be as if tenant B were absent), a hyperproperty no single-execution monitor can decide; the paper measures it as a statistical delta (P95 allocation latency 70.97 -> 50.14 ms) rather than enforcing it. (b) 'reduced resource waste' is an optimization objective, not a safety property - there is no bad prefix to truncate on over-provisioning. A third, weaker split sits in the intent layer: 'agents' ability to declare resource needs and reconstruct execution strategies' makes correct behavior depend on agent cooperation, and the paper concedes 'Declarations are advisory'.

notes:
WHAT THIS PAPER IS. Critical for the adjudicator: AgentCgroup is a SYSTEMS/RESOURCE-MANAGEMENT paper (cs.OS, cs.AI), not a security paper. It contains no threat model, no adversary, no attacker capability, and the words attack/malicious/adversary/credential/untrusted do not appear anywhere in the text. 'Isolation' means noisy-neighbor performance isolation among co-tenant agent sessions. Coding it against ACTION-SURFACE-v1.1 is therefore an off-label application, and every not-covered below means 'the paper does not address this effector', which is exactly what the rubric says to record as not-covered rather than not-applicable. Authors: Zheng, Fan, Fu, Yang, Zhang, Quinn (UC Santa Cruz / Virginia Tech / UConn). Open-source at github.com/eunomia-bpf/agentcgroup.

WHY E2 IS PARTIAL AND NOT COVERED. This is the cell the corpus cares about and the one I am least certain of. The charitable case for a higher score is real: cgroup v2 membership is inherited across fork by the kernel, memcg_bpf_ops is attached to the PARENT cgroup and 'automatically applies to all child cgroups via cgroup v2 hierarchy inheritance', cgroup.freeze 'stops all processes in a subtree', and cgroup.kill 'terminates all processes while handling concurrent forks' - a fork-race-free subtree primitive. That is a genuine, kernel-backed reach to arbitrary descendants, more than most systems in this corpus can say, and it is the single most interesting datum this paper contributes to the E2 descendant question. But it does not make E2 covered, for two independent reasons. FIRST, the reach is to resource ACCOUNTING and TRUNCATION, not to spawn MEDIATION: nothing in AgentCgroup decides whether a subprocess may be created, what binary it runs, or what it does once running. An agent may spawn any descendant it likes; the system only bounds how much memory that descendant may consume. Under the depth rule ('E2 is covered only if descendant spawns are mediated') there is no mediation point at all. SECOND, even the resource reach is granular only on the `bash -c` path, the wrapper's interception key, so the sub-agent tool (17.3% of Haiku tool execution time) and the light tools get no per-call domain. I judged partial rather than not-covered because the hierarchical mechanism demonstrably reaches descendants for the purposes it does serve; an adjudicator who reads the effector strictly as 'spawn permission' should downgrade E2 to not-covered, and I would not argue hard against that.

WHY E5 AND E7 ARE NOT-COVERED DESPITE BEING NAMED. Both appear in the paper only as MEASURED PHENOMENA, never as mediated actions. Package/dependency installation is characterized as a memory consumer (about 10% of Bash time); there is no install-hook mediation and no notion of install-hook network activity, so E5 fails the depth rule outright. The sub-agent tool is characterized (18 s average, 'delegates to a new agent instance') but is explicitly outside the bash wrapper's interception, so E7 gets neither mediation nor a per-call domain. Being measured is not being controlled.

TIER, WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN. The T2/T3 call is the other genuinely close judgment. The paper's kernel enforcement is real and unbypassable from user space ONCE A PROCESS IS IN THE CGROUP - kernel selftests confirm throttle precision within 2.3% relative error on a 2000 ms configured delay. The weakness is upstream of the kernel: cgroup MEMBERSHIP for the per-tool-call domain is established by a user-space bash wrapper keyed on an invocation string. This is precisely the worked example in the rubric (a strong primitive reached through a bypassable hook scores at the hook's tier), so weakest-link forces T3 for the advertised per-tool-call guarantee. I have recorded the T2 residual (workload/container-level memcg, which no user-space bypass escapes) explicitly in cheapestDefeat so an adjudicator can split the cell if the corpus wants to score the two granularities separately. If the corpus scores only the coarsest surviving bound, this is T2.

ADVERSARY PLACEMENT. There is no adversary in the paper, so A1 is an inference from what the evaluation actually stresses: memory pressure arriving from co-located LOW-priority agent sessions outside the protected HIGH-priority workload. A3 is secondary because the intent channel does address an agent that misjudges its own needs ('Declarations are advisory; the feedback loop corrects underestimates') without testing an agent that misdeclares deliberately. A4 is NOT listed: the wrapper and the user-space daemon sit inside the orchestration path, and an adversary there is neither addressed nor tested.

VERSION NOTE. Coded against v3 (22 Jul 2026). The v1 HTML states OS-level execution is 56-74% of end-to-end latency; v3 states 55-60%. I used v3 throughout. All spans are verbatim from the v3 HTML; the only edits are removal of whitespace artifacts introduced by HTML-to-text extraction inside parentheses, and inline multiplication signs (e.g. '15.4x', '50x') render as bare numerals in extraction and are therefore not quoted in any span field.

EVIDENCE GRADE. L2 rather than L1: there is a working C/libbpf prototype on a patched Linux 6.19.0-rc5 kernel, a trace-replay experiment with concrete measured outcomes (100% vs 66% process survival under 1100 MB total for 1233 MB combined demand; 29% P95 allocation-latency reduction; 0.3% P50 overhead), and kernel selftests. Not L3 - no bypass is demonstrated anywhere, by the authors or by me; the bypass in cheapestDefeat is reasoned from the wrapper's stated interception key, not executed. The authors themselves flag the evaluation limit: 'Our current evaluation is limited to trace replay with a proof-of-concept prototype; the characterization covers one agent framework and one benchmark.'
